questions.q: A TS2322 error is reported at order.ts:29:48, under the argument lines in a call. What does that position tell you?
questions.explain: The compiler reports where it noticed the clash. In the lesson the mistake ("ngn") was on another line, and the type that carried it was inferred at the declaration of lines.
options: Line 29 is where two types met and did not fit; the mistake may have been made earlier, where the value got its type
The error is in the function being called
The column is where the file should be edited

questions.q: How should you read the indented "elaboration chain" under a type error's headline?
questions.explain: The headline compares the outermost types (whole arrays or objects). The deepest line names the exact property and the exact clash, which is where to start.
options: Top down: the headline is the most specific part
Bottom up: each indented line goes one level deeper into the types, and the last line is the smallest pair of types that do not fit
Only the headline matters; the rest is noise

questions.q: In the lesson, why did the error say currency: string for both order lines, even the one with "NGN"?
questions.explain: Properties of objects in a variable are mutable, so their literal types widen. Nothing told the compiler to keep "NGN" as a literal until the array met OrderLine[] at the call.
options: TypeScript does not support string literal types in arrays
lines had no declared type, so inference widened each object's currency to string, and the specific mistake ("ngn") was lost at the declaration
JSON strings are always typed as string

questions.q: What does adding satisfies OrderLine[] after the array literal change?
questions.explain: satisfies checks without widening or asserting. as would have hidden the mistake instead. An annotation (const lines: OrderLine[]) also moves the error, but changes the variable's type to OrderLine[].
options: It converts the values to OrderLine at runtime
Each element is checked against OrderLine where it is written, so the error appears on the exact property ("ngn", TS2820 with "Did you mean") while the value keeps its precise type
It has the same effect as as OrderLine[]

questions.q: A build shows TS2307 "Cannot find module '@shop/core'" on line 2, and later a TS18046 "'error' is of type 'unknown'" inside an if (error instanceof DomainError) block. What should you do first?
questions.explain: Failed imports turn everything they provide into error types, and errors cascade from there. Fix the first error, rebuild, then read what is left.
options: Add as DomainError to the later line
Fix the module problem and re-check; the later error is a consequence, because an unresolved DomainError cannot narrow anything
Fix the errors from the bottom of the list up

questions.q: In a terminal without an editor, how can you make tsc print the inferred type of firstPaid?
questions.explain: Nothing is assignable to never, so the compiler reports the value's type in full. typeof at runtime only gives JavaScript's coarse categories such as "object".
options: Add const probe: never = firstPaid;: the error message spells out the full type

questions.q: When is tsc --noEmit --pretty false more useful than the default output?
questions.explain: The pretty format adds code excerpts, squiggles and a summary table, which is easier for people. The plain format keeps each error on one searchable line.
options: When you want exactly one line per error, for grep, scripts or pasting into an issue
When you want the code excerpt under each error
When the project is very small

questions.q: function firstOr<T>(items: T[], fallback: T): T called as firstOr([2500, 1200], "none") reports an error on "none". Why?
questions.explain: The fix depends on the design. If mixed results are intended, give the fallback its own type parameter and return T | F; if not, the error is correct.
options: T was inferred as number from the array, and the fallback was then checked against it
Generic functions cannot take two arguments of the same type parameter
The array should be written with as const

questions.q: const cart = { id: "C-1", skus: [] }; cart.skus.push("RICE-5KG"); fails with "not assignable to parameter of type 'never'". What is the cause?
questions.explain: The word never in a message about an array is the tell. The array can hold nothing, because nobody said what it is for.
options: push is not allowed on object properties
An empty array in an object literal has nothing to infer from, so its type is never[]; annotate it (for example skus: [] as string[])
Strings cannot be stored in arrays inside objects

questions.q: orders.reduce((acc, o) => { acc[o.status] = …; return acc; }, {}) gives TS7053 about indexing type {}. What is the cleanest fix?
questions.explain: reduce infers the accumulator from the initial value, and {} has no properties. A type argument (or an annotated initial value) states the real shape.
options: Tell reduce what you are building: orders.reduce<Record<string, number>>(…, {})

questions.q: createMachine(["pending", "paid"], "shipped") compiles although "shipped" is not a state. What does initial: NoInfer<S> change?
questions.explain: Without it, both arguments are inference sources and S becomes the union of all the strings, so anything fits. Decide which arguments define a type and which are only checked against it.
options: initial no longer contributes candidates for S, so S comes only from the states and "shipped" is checked against it and refused

questions.q: A generic call behaves strangely. Why can passing the type arguments explicitly, such as firstOr<number | string>(…), help you debug it?
questions.explain: If the call works with explicit arguments, inference chose something unexpected; if it still fails, the signature does not allow what you want.
options: It makes the code run faster
It takes inference out of the picture, so you can see whether the problem is in what was inferred or in the function's signature itself
It is required for all generic functions

questions.q: A --traceResolution excerpt starts with "Resolving in CJS mode with conditions 'require', 'types', 'node'" for a file you believed was an ES module. Where do you look?
questions.explain: The mode is decided before any package is searched. Under NodeNext it comes from "type" in the nearest package.json, or from .cts/.mts extensions.
options: At the nearest package.json's "type" field and at the file's extension (.cts/.mts)

questions.q: A trace shows "Matched 'exports' condition 'types'. Using 'exports' subpath '.' with target './dist/index.d.ts'." followed by "File … does not exist." What is wrong?
questions.explain: Each part of the trace rules something out. Reaching the exports map proves the package is installed and the name is right; the missing file is the problem.
options: The package was found and its exports map was read, but the declaration file it points to is missing: not built (workspace) or not published (files)
TypeScript does not support the exports field

questions.q: What is the difference between TS2307 and TS7016 for an import?
questions.explain: TS7016's fix is a declaration (an @types package or your own declare module); TS2307's fix is making the module findable (install, build, publish or fix the path).
options: TS2307: no module was found at all. TS7016: a JavaScript file was found, but there are no types for it
TS2307 is for relative imports, TS7016 for packages

questions.q: --explainFiles says a failing script is in the program because it was "Matched by default include pattern '**/*'". What does that mean?
questions.explain: Decide what belongs to the project: delete or fix the script, or set an explicit "include" such as ["src", "tests"].
options: The tsconfig.json has no include, so every .ts file under the project folder is compiled, including forgotten scripts
The script is a type library

questions.q: tsc --showConfig lists "isolatedModules": true and "incremental": true, which appear in none of your config files. Why?
questions.explain: --showConfig prints the effective configuration after extends and implications, which is what the compiler really uses.
options: They are TypeScript's defaults for every project
They are implied by other options you set: verbatimModuleSyntax implies isolatedModules, and composite implies incremental

questions.q: You changed a function, but running the program still shows the old behaviour. The type check passes. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explain: Check which file actually runs and when it was written. Deleting dist and rebuilding from clean, as CI does, removes the whole class of problem.
options: The program runs stale output: an old dist build, or a stray compiled .js next to the source that is loaded instead

questions.q: Code type-checks in your editor but fails in CI. Which check comes first?
questions.explain: Editors often use their own bundled TypeScript, or pick up a different config file for the open file. Differences in version or settings explain most "works here, fails there" type errors.
options: Compare npx tsc -v in both places, and whether the editor uses the same tsconfig.json (--showConfig in CI)

questions.q: A program with a clean type check computes a wildly wrong total because a number field arrived as a string. Where do you look for the cause?
questions.explain: If the types are consistent and the value is wrong, a type was claimed rather than checked somewhere. Replace that claim with a runtime check at the boundary.
options: At the escape hatches where outside data got its type: as casts, any, !, @ts-ignore, JSON.parse and hand-written declarations

questions.q: The compiler reports a possible undefined that "cannot happen" in practice. What does the lesson recommend before reaching for ! or as?
questions.explain: An assertion records nothing about why it is safe; a better type or a checking assertion function does, and it keeps protecting the code after future changes.
options: Try to express why it cannot happen in the types (a narrower parameter, a discriminated union, or an assertion function that checks), so the reason is kept for the next person

questions.q: For orders declared as const with statuses "paid" and "pending", the probe showed that orders.find((o) => o.status === "paid") has the type of the paid order only (or undefined). Why?
questions.explain: Since TypeScript 5.5 a simple boolean callback like this is treated as a type guard. Probing the type showed a precise result that guessing would have missed.
options: find always returns the first element's type
TypeScript inferred a type predicate from the callback: it can only return true for the order whose literal status is "paid", so the result is narrowed
It is a bug in TypeScript

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The value is the string "250000", so + concatenates. The type said number because of the as Order cast, so the compiler saw nothing wrong.
options: TypeError: cannot add a string to a number

questions.q: Continuing from the last question, the receipt divides by 100. What does this print?
questions.explain: Division converts the concatenated string "250000150000" back to a number, so the bad value looks like a real, huge amount. Bugs from escape hatches often travel far before they show.
questions.code:
const totalKobo = ("250000" as unknown as number) + 150_000;
console.log(`₦${(totalKobo / 100).toFixed(2)}`);
options: TypeError: toFixed is not a function

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: ?? only replaces null and undefined, so 0 is kept. An empty array gives undefined for items[0], and a null first item is replaced too, which may or may not be what the design wants.

questions.q: This version compiles because S is inferred from both arguments. What does it print?
questions.explain: Nothing checks the initial state at runtime, and the too-generous inference let the compiler accept it. NoInfer fixes the type side; a runtime check is still wise if the states come from data.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The type argument only fixed the compile-time type of the accumulator. At runtime, keys appear in the order they were first set, and repeated statuses add up.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: find returns the first match. Its type is narrowed to the two paid orders (or undefined), so the ?. is still needed.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The ! is erased; it checks nothing. The crash happens one step later, when a property is read from undefined, which is why a ! is one of the escape hatches to search for.
options:
delivery 150000
insurance Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'kobo')

questions.q: What does this boundary check print?
questions.explain: Checking at the boundary turns a far-away wrong total into an immediate, specific message with the bad value in it. JSON.stringify(undefined) is undefined, so the missing field shows as undefined.
options:
250000
expected whole kobo, got "250000"
expected whole kobo, got 2500.5
expected whole kobo, got undefined

250000
250000
expected whole kobo, got 2500.5
expected whole kobo, got undefined

250000
expected whole kobo, got "250000"
2500.5
expected whole kobo, got undefined

250000
expected whole kobo, got 250000
expected whole kobo, got 2500.5
expected whole kobo, got null

questions.q: The lesson's escape-hatch scanner uses /\bas\s+(?!const\b)[A-Z]\w*/ for casts. Which lines does it report?
questions.explain: The pattern wants a capitalised type name after as, so as unknown as number (lower-case built-in types) slips through, although it is the most dangerous cast of all. A regular expression is a start for a review; real tools use the compiler's syntax tree.

questions.q: Replace the cast with a check. Write parseOrder(json) that returns { id: string; totalKobo: number } only if id is a string and totalKobo is a whole, non-negative number, and otherwise throws a TypeError whose message names the field and shows the bad value with JSON.stringify.
questions.explain: The only cast left is from unknown to a record of unknown values, which claims nothing about the fields; every field is then checked before it is trusted. The returned object is built from checked values, so extra fields in the JSON are dropped too.

questions.q: Write deepestLine(error): given the text of one pretty tsc error, return the most specific line of its elaboration chain, meaning the last line (trimmed) of the first block of lines, before the first empty line.
questions.explain: The chain ends at the first blank line, where the code excerpt begins. For an error without a chain, the headline is itself the most specific line. Reading this line first is the habit the lesson recommends.
questions.expected:
Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'Currency'.
cart.ts:2:16 - error TS2345: Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'never'.

questions.q: Write parseErrorLine(line) for one-line tsc --pretty false output such as src/app.ts(4,29): error TS2307: Cannot find module '@shop/logger'., returning { file, line, column, code, message } (line and column as numbers), or null for any other line. Then count errors per code.
questions.explain: The one-line format is made for tools. Counting by code shows at a glance that most errors are "cannot find module", which, as the lesson showed, usually means one build problem, not many code problems.

questions.q: Write diagnose(trace): scan a --traceResolution excerpt and return "not installed" if it never found a package.json for the package, "missing file: <path>" for the first "File '…' does not exist." after the package was found, and "resolved" if a line says "was successfully resolved".
questions.explain: This is the lesson's reading order as code: did it find the package, and if so, which promised file was missing? The same questions work by eye on a real, much longer trace.

questions.q: Rewrite firstOr so that the fallback can be a different type from the items, and the result type is the union of the two. Then change both calls to use the fallback "none", which must compile.
questions.explain: With two type parameters, each argument is a source for its own type, and neither is checked against the other. The return type T | F tells callers the truth: they may get either.

questions.q: Make createMachine safe twice over: use NoInfer so the compiler rejects an unknown literal initial state, and add a runtime check that throws Error("unknown initial state: <state>") for states that come from data (where the type is just string).
questions.explain: NoInfer protects literal calls at compile time; the runtime check protects values the compiler cannot see, such as configuration. Types and checks cover different gaps.

questions.q: Fix the accumulator typing so that this compiles, and print the number of orders per status as paid=2 pending=1.
questions.explain: The type argument on reduce gives the accumulator its real shape from the start, instead of the empty {} of the initial value.

questions.q: Improve the escape-hatch scanner so that it also reports as unknown as double casts (as "double cast") and @ts-expect-error without a reason (the directive followed by nothing but spaces, as "bare expect-error"). Print line N: kinds for each line with findings.
questions.explain: as unknown as T forces any value into any type and deserves the closest review. A @ts-expect-error with a written reason can be checked by a reviewer; a bare one can hide an error nobody meant to accept.
questions.expected:
line 1: as
line 2: double cast
line 3: bare expect-error
